Why does this matter? Because the regression framework is far more flexible. With a simple change to the model formula, you can add control variables, test multiple CTAs simultaneously, or look for subgroup effects — all while producing the same correct inference in the simple case.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
Imagine your boss is impatient. Instead of waiting for all 1,000 visitors per group, she wants to check the results every 100 visitors. If any of those 10 interim tests hits \(p < 0.05\), she wants to declare a winner and stop.
This practice — commonly called peeking — is one of the most widespread mistakes in A/B testing. A single test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% false positive rate. But each peek is another independent chance to get lucky in the wrong direction. Across 10 peeks, the cumulative probability of at least one false positive climbs well above 5%.
Let’s demonstrate this. We set up a world where there is no true difference (\(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\), so \(\theta = 0\)), then simulate 10,000 experiments:

np.random.seed(123)
n_experiments = 10000
peek_points = np.arange(100, 1001, 100)

false_positive_peek = np.zeros(n_experiments, dtype=bool)
false_positive_single = np.zeros(n_experiments, dtype=bool)

for i in range(n_experiments):
    A_null = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)
    B_null = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)

    for k in peek_points:
        pA = A_null[:k].mean()
        pB = B_null[:k].mean()
        se_k = np.sqrt(pA*(1-pA)/k + pB*(1-pB)/k)
        if se_k == 0:
            continue
        if 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs((pA - pB) / se_k))) < 0.05:
            false_positive_peek[i] = True
            break

    pA_f, pB_f = A_null.mean(), B_null.mean()
    se_f = np.sqrt(pA_f*(1-pA_f)/1000 + pB_f*(1-pB_f)/1000)
    if se_f > 0:
        false_positive_single[i] = (
            2*(1-stats.norm.cdf(abs((pA_f-pB_f)/se_f))) < 0.05
        )

fp_peek_rate = false_positive_peek.mean()
fp_single_rate = false_positive_single.mean()

print(f"Single-test FP rate: {fp_single_rate:.3f}")
print(f"Peeking FP rate:     {fp_peek_rate:.3f}")

Single-test FP rate: 0.052
Peeking FP rate:     0.199

A single end-of-experiment test produces a false positive rate right around the promised 5%. But peeking 10 times inflates it to around {fp_peek_rate:.0%} — roughly three times the nominal level.
In practice, this means a company running A/B tests with peeking will regularly declare winners that don’t exist. The fix? Commit to your sample size before running the experiment and test exactly once at the end. If early stopping is genuinely necessary, use methods designed for it — like sequential testing or the Bonferroni correction — which account for multiple looks explicitly.

What the paper studies
In April 1992, New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05/hr while neighboring Pennsylvania kept its minimum unchanged. Card and Krueger surveyed 410 fast-food restaurants (Burger King, KFC, Roy Rogers, Wendy’s) in both states shortly before and about eight months after the increase, then used a difference-in-differences design to estimate the employment effect. The conventional prediction — that a binding minimum wage reduces employment — would have NJ employment fall relative to PA. Instead, the authors find the opposite: employment at NJ stores rose slightly relative to PA stores, yielding a positive (statistically weak) treatment effect on full-time-equivalent employment.
FTE is defined as full-time workers + 0.5 × part-time workers + managers. So a store with 10 full-timers, 8 part-timers, and 2 managers counts as 10 + 4 + 2 = 16 FTE.

The NJ coefficient is 2.326 with OLS standard error 1.192, against the paper’s 2.33 (1.19). Point estimate and standard error both match essentially exactly. The coefficient reads as “NJ stores gained roughly 2.3 FTE per store relative to PA stores after the minimum wage rose,” and is marginally significant under OLS (t ≈ 1.95, so the 95% CI just barely touches zero).

title: marketing analytics
text:
Additional — robust standard errors
The paper reports plain OLS standard errors, which assume residual variance is constant across stores. That assumption is suspect here on inspection alone: a store employing 40 FTE has far more room to swing by ±5 workers than a store employing 10. Splitting the Table 4 sample at the median baseline FTE (19.5) makes the asymmetry concrete — residual variance is 41.7 among small stores versus 102.2 among large stores, a ratio of 2.45×. That’s textbook heteroskedasticity.
Heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC1) standard errors are the minimal fix. The HC1 standard error on the NJ coefficient is 1.452 — about 22% larger than the OLS 1.192. Under HC1, the coefficient is no longer significant at conventional levels (t ≈ 1.60, p ≈ 0.11). The point estimate — the core finding — is unchanged. But inference tightens from “marginally positive” to “statistically indistinguishable from zero” once heteroskedasticity is allowed in.



OLS vs HC1 95% CIs on the NJ coefficient. Same point estimate, different inference: OLS just barely excludes zero, HC1 clearly does not.


This doesn’t overturn Card & Krueger’s broader evidence — the 1994 paper rests on many specifications, including the wage-gap regressions in Table 4 columns iii–v, and the book-length follow-up marshalls much more. But it does illustrate how sensitive the headline t-statistic is to a standard-error choice that rarely gets discussed in pop summaries of the result. Clustering by chain was considered and rejected — only four chains is too few for cluster-robust inference to be well-behaved.

title: marketing analytics
text:
So what
The Card & Krueger point estimate is remarkably robust: it survives different samples, different software, different standard-error assumptions. What doesn’t survive is the clean “NJ employment went up, and it was statistically significant” story, at least not under HC1. The coefficient is still positive, the direction still counterintuitive — but under the more defensible variance assumption, the estimate stops being distinguishable from zero. Whether you call that “the effect is positive but noisily measured” or “the effect is effectively zero” says more about your priors than about the data.

section: The measurement was correct. The model was broken.
text:
The measurement was correct. The model was broken.
Every metric embeds a theory — an implicit claim about what the number means. DAU is a proxy for engagement. Engagement is a proxy for value delivered. Value delivered is a proxy for willingness to pay. Willingness to pay is a proxy for revenue.
When DAU went up, the team assumed the whole chain held. It didn’t. Users were active but not finding value. They were clicking around, confused. Confusion generates activity. Activity looks like engagement. Engagement looks like growth.
The metric was accurate. The theory behind it was wrong.

title: marketing analytics
text:
We mistake precision for validity
A thermometer can tell you the temperature in a room to two decimal places. That doesn’t tell you if the room is comfortable for a human being. We’ve built a data culture that is obsessed with precision but careless about validity.
Precision is a property of measurement. Validity is a property of the relationship between the measurement and what you actually care about. You can have one without the other. Most dashboards optimize for precision and assume validity.

title: marketing analytics
text:
The question that fixes it
Before you build any metric, ask: what decision does this change?
If DAU goes up by 10%, what do you do differently? If the answer is “we celebrate and keep doing what we’re doing,” the metric isn’t driving decisions — it’s decorating them. You’re not measuring to learn. You’re measuring to confirm.
The useful metrics are the ones that make you act asymmetrically. High number → one action. Low number → different action. If both outcomes lead to the same plan, the metric is noise dressed as signal.

title: marketing analytics
text:
Dashboards are not understanding
A dashboard shows you what happened. It says nothing about why. And it is completely silent on what to do next.
Understanding requires a model — a causal story about the world. Dashboards show you symptoms. Models explain mechanisms. Most teams invest heavily in dashboards and lightly in models, then wonder why they keep being surprised.
The dashboard that lied wasn’t broken. The team’s mental model of what it meant was.

Measurement is a tool for thinking, not a substitute for it.

Zero Bootstrap, zero Quarto defaults. theme: none + minimal: true in _quarto.yml. Every pixel is authored.

title: Design System
text:
Zero Bootstrap, zero Quarto defaults. theme: none + minimal: true in _quarto.yml. Every pixel is authored.
Dark-first, light as a refined variant. Dark mode is the default (set pre-paint in _partials/head-extras.html via inline <script>); light mode adds targeted overrides in a single html:not(.dark) block at the end of the CSS.
Liquid glass aesthetic on .navbar, .badge, .theme-pill, .cell:not(.terminal-cell), .copy-btn, .btn-primary (dark). Terminal is explicitly opaque — it represents a code environment, not a UI panel.
Gradient = identity. Blue→violet (#3B82F6 → #A78BFA) appears in accents, hover shadows, splash buttons, project card glow. Layered box-shadow fakes gradient borders without border-image (which conflicts with border-radius).
Zero JS dependencies. Vanilla fetch() for JSON data, vanilla mousemove listeners for the cursor effects.

title: marketing analytics
section: Why Do We Need to Optimize?
text:
Why Do We Need to Optimize?


Maximum Likelihood Estimation asks:

“What parameter value makes my observed data most probable?”

\[\hat{\theta} = \underset{\theta}{\arg\max} \; \ell(\theta \mid \mathbf{x})\]

Closed-form solutions exist for simple models (Poisson, Gaussian)
For complex models (logistic, mixture, neural nets) → no formula
We need an algorithm to climb to the peak








The core idea
The log-likelihood is a surface. MLE means finding the top of that surface.




Think of it like hiking in fog — you can’t see the peak, but you can always feel which way is uphill.

title: Climbing the Likelihood Mountain
text:
The Landscape: A Log-Likelihood Surface


Example: Normal model, estimating \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\)
\[\ell(\mu,\sigma) = -\tfrac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(x_i-\mu)^2\]


Two parameters → 2D surface
The peak = MLE \((\hat{\mu},\, \hat{\sigma})\)
The gradient \(\nabla \ell\) points uphill — telling us which way to step

title: Climbing the Likelihood Mountain
text:
The Algorithm: Gradient Ascent


Update rule — repeat until convergence:
\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} + \alpha \cdot \nabla_\theta \, \ell\!\left(\theta^{(t)}\right)\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(\theta^{(t)}\)
Current parameter estimate


\(\alpha\)
Learning rate (step size)


\(\nabla_\theta \ell\)
Gradient — which way is uphill




Stop when the slope flattens: \(\|\nabla\ell\| < \varepsilon\)


# Gradient Ascent — Poisson MLE
lam   = 0.5    # initial guess
alpha = 0.15   # learning rate

for step in range(100):
    grad = sum(x) / lam - n
    lam  = lam + alpha * grad

    if abs(grad) < 1e-4:
        break

# converges to lam ≈ x̄  (true MLE)

The Catch: Learning Rate Matters



α too large Overshoots, oscillates, diverges

α just right ✓ Smooth, fast convergence

α too small Converges, but painfully slow


In practice: adaptive optimizers like Adam and L-BFGS tune \(\alpha\) automatically — this is why they dominate in real ML pipelines.

section: The Problem: When There’s No Formula
text:
The Problem: When There’s No Formula


Maximum Likelihood Estimation asks:

“What parameter values make my observed data most probable?”

\[\hat{\theta} = \underset{\theta}{\arg\max} \; \ell(\theta \mid \mathbf{x})\]

Simple models (Poisson, Gaussian) → closed-form solution
Complex models (logistic regression, MNL) → no formula
We need an algorithm to climb to the peak





The Core Idea
The log-likelihood is a surface. MLE = finding the top of that surface.




Think of it like hiking in fog — you can’t see the peak, but you can always feel which way is uphill.
